title: Nvidia Stock Has More Than 60% Upside According to Analysts' Average Price Target. Should You Buy While the AI Trade Wobbles?
detail:
Nvidia Stock Has More Than 60% Upside According to Analysts' Average Price Target. Should You Buy While the AI Trade Wobbles?
Chris Neiger, The Motley Fool
Sat, November 7, 2026 at 12:20 PM CST 5 min read
NVDA

Investors are skeptical of many AI stocks right now, questioning the long-term return on investment for tech companies spending so much on data center infrastructure. And as a leading semiconductor company for AI infrastructure, Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) has felt the pain from the sell-off, with its share price falling 13% over the past month.

That's put Nvidia's share price at around $202, far below analysts' average price target for Nvidia stock of $327. If it reaches that target, investors stand to gain around 62%. So, is now the right time to buy Nvidia stock, despite the concerns about AI spending?

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

I think so, especially given that recent tech earnings reports indicate tech companies are likely to continue investing in infrastructure over the next few years.

Image source: The Motley Fool.
AI spending continues to ramp up

Let's start with SK Hynix's (NASDAQ: SKHY) recently reported third-quarter results. The company is the leading high-bandwidth (HBM) memory company with 50% market share and the second-largest DRAM and NAND flash memory company with 24% and 19% market share, respectively.

The company has benefited immensely from a ramp-up in AI spending, sending its sales 328% higher in the quarter and its operating profit up 632%. Even more impressive is that the company's management said in a press release that 50% of its available memory supply for 2027-2028 is already sold out -- and that it expects its supply to remain constrained through 2030.

What does this have to do with Nvidia? Well, SK Hynix is the leading supplier of HBM memory for many of Nvidia's data center components. If SK Hynix is experiencing exponential demand for its memory processors, part of that is due to Nvidia placing substantial orders. And if Nvidia is placing large orders for memory, it's because AI spending continues to rise.

This leads me to Alphabet's and Microsoft's recent cloud sales. These two companies hold a combined 35% of the cloud market, and they're both experiencing impressive sales gains from their AI spending. Google Cloud revenue more than doubled in the third quarter to $30.7 billion and Microsoft's Azure sales rose 48% to $33.2 billion.

Alphabet says it will spend up to $205 billion this year in capital expenditures (capex), mostly for AI. Microsoft says it will spend $170 billion in fiscal 2027. That's an acceleration of spending for both companies and it's a result of Microsoft and Alphabet realizing that their cloud investments are paying off.

title: Did Apple Just Get a Boost From Democrats? Data Center Moratoriums Could Benefit the iPhone Maker
detail:
Did Apple Just Get a Boost From Democrats? Data Center Moratoriums Could Benefit the iPhone Maker
Adam Levy, The Motley Fool
Sat, November 7, 2026 at 1:23 PM CST 5 min read
AAPL
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL) issued a warning to investors when it shared its fourth-quarter earnings results at the start of November. Its huge profit margin on device sales could head in the wrong direction for the foreseeable future. The culprit: memory chips.

Memory chip pricing has soared over the past few quarters, driven by growth in AI data center spending. AI accelerator chips get packaged alongside high-bandwidth memory chips, which are effectively stacks of standard DRAM memory chips -- the same types of chips found in Apple's iPhone and MacBook, among other devices. Demand for those chips, while supply remains limited, has led to massive price increases, and Apple is finally starting to feel the pain.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

The recent election, however, could provide some relief for Apple, given the growing potential for Democrats to impose AI data center moratoriums across the country.

Image source: Getty Images.
Delays in data centers could open up more supply for Apple

Democrats took control of both the House and the Senate in this year's midterm election, paving the way for more federal regulation and policies that could curb the growth of AI. The more immediate impact, however, could come at the state level. Four of the biggest states for AI data center developments -- Texas, Ohio, Georgia, and Arizona -- will have Democratic governors once they're sworn in in January.

Many of those governors have announced plans to increase oversight and regulation of new data center construction (Texas did so even before Tuesday's election), aiming to mitigate any negative impacts on citizens. Venture Capitalist Brad Gerstner suggested that 25% to 35% of next year's data center build-out could be at risk of delays as a result of new governments across the country.

That could provide some relief for Apple. If data centers aren't going under construction, that means there's no place to put new server racks, and less demand for high-bandwidth memory chips. Reduced demand should put downward pressure on prices, limiting the impact of memory chip pricing on Apple's gross margin.

Apple management danced around whether it had already locked in pricing for some memory supply. All three major memory chipmakers, Micron, SK Hynix, and Samsung, have shifted to signing long-term agreements to establish pricing ranges and provide more confidence in building new capacity. While that caps their near-term upside, it protects them from a major price collapse as they work to increase the total supply of memory chips.

Think It's Too Late to Buy Cloudflare Stock? Here's the 1 Reason Why There's Still Time

Cloudflare (NYSE: NET) stock has gained roughly 280% over the past three years through Nov. 5, 2026. But it could still reward patient investors for one reason: The business remains small compared with the market management is targeting.

Cloudflare helps businesses keep their websites, applications, and networks fast and secure. At its June 9 investor day, management estimated a $238 billion addressable market for 2026, based on Gartner research. That's the potential annual spending in the markets its products serve, not a revenue forecast. Management projects that opportunity will reach $384 billion by 2029.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Against that backdrop, Cloudflare expects its full-year 2026 revenue to be nearly $3 billion -- representing only about 1% of the addressable market. It doesn't need to dominate every market it serves to become a much larger business. Winning even a modest share of that spending could support years of growth.

Image source: Getty Images.
Priced for growth, but still early

Cloudflare is growing rapidly. Third-quarter revenue grew 39% year over year to $783 million -- its fastest growth in nearly four years. Management expects fourth-quarter revenue to be up about 38% year over year, indicating strong momentum heading into 2027.

The stock is priced for growth, trading at 34 times trailing sales as of Nov. 5. Companies operating in an expanding market and growing revenue rapidly are usually worth holding at a premium. With just a tiny fraction of its opportunity captured, it's not too late to buy the stock. It looks more like a company in the early stages of growth than one nearing maturity.

title: MercadoLibre's Profits Fall Again. What It Means for Investors
detail:
MercadoLibre's Profits Fall Again. What It Means for Investors
Jeremy Bowman, The Motley Fool
Sat, November 7, 2026 at 1:05 PM CST 4 min read
MELI
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

MercadoLibre (NASDAQ:MELI) delivered another round of strong top-line growth, but falling profits again sank the stock.

Shares fell 12% on Thursday as investors have grown impatient with the company's investment cycle, as it spends on lower free shipping thresholds, expanded logistics, and growing its credit business. However, that again led to narrower margins.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Revenue in the quarter jumped 45% to $10.75 billion, edging out estimates of $10.71 billion. Both core businesses delivered strong growth, with gross merchandise volume up 38% to $23 billion, and total payment volume jumped 53% to $109 billion.

Operating income in the quarter fell from $636 million to $601 million, and the company reported a net income margin of just 4.2%. On a per-share basis, earnings rose from $8.32 to $8.83 as the company benefited from lower tax expense. Still, that was below analyst estimates at $9.27.

MercadoLibre doesn't give guidance, so estimates are a bit of a guessing game, which works against the stock at times like these when it's investing in the business.

Image source: Getty Images.

Are its investments paying off?

The top-line metrics are clearly moving in the right direction, and management said it gained share in its three largest markets, Brazil, Mexico, and Argentina, which should quell concerns about competition from Amazon and Sea Limited's Shopee.

Importantly, the company continued to see engagement strengthening, and it sees a significant opportunity to grow purchase frequency, noting that its buyers make an average of 12 purchases a year, compared to more than 50 for e-commerce shoppers in developed countries. Faster shipping, lowering the free shipping threshold, and expanding its selection are part of its strategy to build a sticky habit and strengthen its competitive advantage, much like Amazon has done in the U.S.

The company is also seeing more customers adopt multiple products, which drive both revenue and margin improvement over the long run. As the business has scaled up, its cost per shipment in Brazil has fallen, down 5% in constant currency over the last year and 14% since the first quarter of 2025, a sign that it's effectively scaling its logistics operations.

Its credit card portfolio has been another source of headwinds on the bottom line, as the company needs to book a provision for expected losses when it issues new cards, even before it's earned any profits. The credit portfolio grew 62% to $18 billion in the quarter, and default and interest metrics remained stable.

title: Eli Lilly Just Raised Its 2026 Revenue Forecast by $5.5 Billion. Is the Stock Still a Buy?

Eli Lilly Just Raised Its 2026 Revenue Forecast by $5.5 Billion. Is the Stock Still a Buy?

Sat, November 7, 2026 at 12:50 PM CST 5 min read

NVDA

Trading disclosure

After a 57% run-up over the past 52 weeks, Eli Lilly (NYSE: LLY) shares are expensive. The stock is now trading at 47 times trailing earnings. That's more than double the price-to-earnings ratio of the pharmaceutical industry. There are some sound reasons for that, which, put together, make the stock a buy, in my opinion.

First, sales are growing rapidly. Revenue was $24.4 billion in the third quarter, 39% higher than the same period a year ago. Profits are soaring, too. Earnings per share increased 16% in the quarter, to $7.22. Even better, management raised its guidance for full-year revenue from $85 billion to $87 billion to $91 billion to $92 billion.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

It's no wonder, as Lilly's GLP-1 drug tirzepatide, which is marketed as Mounjaro for type 2 diabetes and Zepbound for obesity, dethroned Merck's cancer drug Keytruda last year to become the world's best-selling drug.

In the third quarter, Zepbound sales climbed 49% to about $5.4 billion, while Mounjaro sales jumped 65% to more than $10.7 billion. Foundayo, an oral weight-loss drug, contributed sales of $184 million in the quarter.

New markets and use cases for GLP-1 drugs

I believe those numbers are just the beginning. Morgan Stanley forecasts that the market for obesity drugs will reach $190 billion by 2035, more than double its 2025 level. Right now, that growth is being driven by new oral treatments, expected to be adopted by consumers at a faster pace than injection-based delivery systems, and by expanded coverage from Medicare, the largest payer for healthcare services in the U.S.

Even those predictions may fall well short of the actual market for GLP-1 drugs. That's because medical researchers continue to find new uses for the drugs beyond obesity and weight loss. GLP-1s are beginning to look like miracle drugs that will cause a tectonic shift in the healthcare industry.

First, there are international markets, largely untapped so far (outside of Europe). Morgan Stanley estimates there are more than 1 billion people with obesity living outside the U.S. To date, adoption in foreign markets has been constrained by several factors, including affordability, needle aversion, and safety concerns -- all of which can be overcome. The investment bank's research mentions Brazil and China, in particular.

title: Where Will Rigetti Computing Stock Be in 3 Years?
detail:
Where Will Rigetti Computing Stock Be in 3 Years?
Anders Bylund, The Motley Fool

RGTI
IONQ
NVDA

Trading disclosure

As of Nov. 6, Rigetti Computing (NASDAQ: RGTI) stock is down 48.1% in 2026. That's not a typo, and it's not the first quantum stock I've watched do this.

The shares fell 18.7% over the past month, mostly because the whole group got dragged down when quantum computing rival IonQ (NYSE: IONQ) announced a $2.0 billion equity offering in mid-October. Investors sold the whole pile, including Rigetti. The stock traded at more than 300 times trailing sales at the time, and there's not much room for error on those lofty heights.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

The sell-off hit the whole group, even companies with little direct exposure to the offering.

Government money, with strings attached

Rigetti's most significant recent development is a letter of intent with the U.S. Department of Commerce for up to $100.0 million over three years, aimed at superconducting quantum research under the CHIPS Act. The deal is not definitive yet.

The government would receive an equity stake, which means new shares. Existing shareholders would face share dilution if and when the deal closes.

Coherence time is the bottleneck

Rigetti's headline numbers are fine. Q2 revenue hit $5.1 million, up from $1.8 million, mostly from on-premises Novera sales. The company's flagship 108-qubit chip runs at about 99.1% median two-qubit fidelity, which sounds great until you remember the three-year goal is 99.9% -- nearly a whole order of magnitude tighter.

Management says the holdup is coherence time, meaning how long a qubit can keep its quantum state before information is lost. That figure is 25 to 30 microseconds in Rigetti's systems. Management hopes to double or triple it over several years, but lab results don't always carry over to production chips.

"Coherence time is the limiting factor for 2-qubit gate fidelity at this time, and that's why we are so focused on improving coherence time," CEO Subodh Kulkarni said on the Q2 earnings call.

Image source: Getty Images.
Three years is the right test

Rigetti has committed to a three-year roadmap, and that window is the most useful yardstick for investors. If it reaches the stated fidelity and scale targets around 2029, the stock's current valuation could look more reasonable in hindsight. But if it misses one or more of the official goals, a stock priced this high has a long way to fall.

title: Jim Cramer sends a strong signal to Nvidia stock investors
detail:
Jim Cramer sends a strong signal to Nvidia stock investors
Hillary Remy
Sat, November 7, 2026 at 11:17 AM CST 4 min read
NVDA
AMD
AVGO
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Nvidia has gone from Wall Street's favorite stock to one of its most heavily sold stocks in just a few weeks. Shares have dropped about 22% over the past month, and Wednesday's session was ugly. The stock closed at $186.24, down nearly 7% on the day, as a broad sell-off hit the chip sector hard. AMD fell more than 17% and Broadcom dropped more than 10%.

Jim Cramer, the host of CNBC's Mad Money, spent part of his Wednesday program making the case that now is the time to buy. His argument rests on valuation: "This is the cheapest multiple on Nvidia in about a decade. We're at 16.5 now." He said investors are writing off a company he believes remains the dominant force in artificial intelligence infrastructure, 24/7 Wall St. reported.

What sparked the Nvidia selloff

The slide started in late September. At that point, Nvidia's shares sat at about 17 times forward earnings, a level not seen since January 2015.

Also read: Jim Cramer sends clear signal on Apple and Palantir stock

The stock's 15-year average is roughly 30 times. The discount was real, but sellers kept coming anyway.

The trigger on Wednesday appears to have been a mix of concerns: worries about AI regulation, questions over whether hyperscalers will keep spending at the pace Nvidia needs, and rotation out of high-multiple tech names. The selloff was broad enough to drag down the entire chip sector, not just Nvidia.

Nvidia's fundamentals tell a different story

The business results themselves have been hard to fault. In its fiscal second quarter, Nvidia posted revenue of $96.2 billion, up sharply from a year earlier. Data center revenue came in at $89 billion, a 117% jump. Earnings of $2.22 a share beat the $2.09 consensus estimate. The company guided for fiscal third-quarter revenue of $108 billion, a figure that left some investors expecting more, according to Nvidia.

The company has also been using its cash aggressively. Nvidia repurchased about $39.8 billion worth of its own stock in the first half of fiscal 2027, and it still had $99 billion left on its buyback authorization at the end of the second quarter. Total buyback capacity, including a new tranche approved in late September, now stands at $235 billion, Cramer noted on X.

Related: Whirlpool delivers bad news to customers before Black Friday

Cash on the balance sheet stood at $56.6 billion. Supply commitments have more than doubled, from $119 billion to $279 billion, a sign that the company is locking in future production at scale. Revenue from the roughly 50 largest frontier AI labs alone accounts for about $50 billion of that pipeline, the Motley Fool reported.

3 Dividend Stocks I'd Buy With $5,000 Before the End of November

Dividend stocks can turn savings into a growing stream of income. If I had $5,000 to invest in dividend stocks before the end of November, I'd split it equally among PepsiCo (NASDAQ: PEP), Hershey (NYSE: HSY), and Home Depot (NYSE: HD).

All three have long records of paying dividends, and research shows that companies that pay dividends have historically outperformed those that don't. According to Hartford Funds and Ned Davis Research, S&P 500 stocks that grew or initiated dividends returned about 10% per year from 1973 through 2025, versus about 4% for stocks that paid no dividends.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

At Nov. 3 prices, investing $1,667 into each stock would earn about $176 a year in dividends, a blended yield of about 3.5% -- more than three times the S&P 500 average. Here's why now is a good time to buy these stocks.

Image source: Getty Images.
PepsiCo: $71 in income

PepsiCo sells some of the world's best-known snacks and drinks, from Doritos to Gatorade. A $1,667 investment would buy about 12 shares at current prices, yielding about $71 per year based on Pepsi's current annualized dividend of $5.92 per share.

The business is gaining momentum, especially overseas. Organic revenue, which excludes the impact of foreign currency fluctuations, grew 3% year over year in the third quarter -- the highest rate of growth since the fourth quarter of 2023. The international business performed well, with organic revenue up 8%.

PepsiCo is also cutting costs to fund more growth. CEO Ramon Laguarta said additional structural cost reductions "will be implemented in the coming months to help fund investments that aim to accelerate organic revenue growth."

The stock yields about 4.3%, and the dividend accounted for about 75% of trailing free cash flow (cash from operations minus business investments). This year marked PepsiCo's 54th consecutive annual dividend increase, making it a Dividend King (a category of companies that have increased their dividends for at least 50 years without interruption).

With international growth looking strong and management focused on reducing costs, Pepsi's high yield looks very attractive.

Hershey: $58 in income

Hershey owns iconic treats like Reese's and Kit Kat, plus fast-growing salty snacks like Dot's pretzels. A $1,667 stake buys almost 10 shares, which would pay about $58 a year based on the annualized dividend of $5.808 per share.
